summary: Year 6 learners (ages 10-11) build the quadrilateral hierarchy from properties rather than appearance, grasping two load-bearing ideas: attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus an extra constraint) and the asymmetry of class inclusion (all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares). The target understanding is the van Hiele informal-deduction level (level 3 when levels are numbered from 1, level 2 when numbered from 0): learners justify and defend subset links from properties, overcoming the exclusive/oblong prototype formed in earlier school years and the tendency to treat 'all A are B' as symmetric.
misconceptions: Treating 'all squares are rectangles' as symmetric — concluding 'so all rectangles are squares' (or that both are equally true/false)
Reversing the subset direction — thinking a rectangle is a special square rather than a square a special rectangle
Exclusive/oblong prototype persisting from KS2: a 'real' rectangle must be longer than it is wide, so a square is not a rectangle at all
Not applying inheritance: agreeing a rhombus is a parallelogram in words, but not granting that it therefore has all parallelogram properties (e.g. opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisecting)

activities.title: Build the shape by adding properties
steps: Start with a general 'floppy' quadrilateral and switch on one property at a time: make opposite sides parallel, add right angles, make all sides equal.

Watch how the shape changes and where it belongs: making opposite sides parallel turns it into a parallelogram; adding right angles makes it a rectangle; instead making all sides equal makes it a rhombus; doing both makes it a square.

After each change, record in a property table which properties the shape now has (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals), noticing that these ticks accumulate as you go down each branch of the family tree.

Attempt the reverse challenge: try to make a rectangle that is NOT a parallelogram, and explain why you cannot — four right angles force each pair of opposite sides to be parallel (two sides that are both perpendicular to the same side are parallel), so every rectangle automatically meets the parallelogram definition.
Place the finished square, rhombus and rectangle onto a family-tree (hierarchy) diagram and into nested Venn sets, saying why the square sits inside BOTH the rhombus and rectangle regions.
activities.insight: A square inherits every property of the parallelogram, rhombus and rectangle because it is a special case of each; adding an extra constraint moves a shape DOWN the hierarchy, and the inheritance runs one way only — removing the extra property moves back up, but you cannot have a rectangle that is not also a parallelogram.

activities.title: Defend the asymmetry: which statement is true?
steps: Consider two statements: (1) all squares are rectangles, (2) all rectangles are squares. Decide which is true and which is false.

Justify the choice from properties: a square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) PLUS all four sides equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle; a rectangle only becomes a square when it also has equal sides, which most do not.
Test the everyday analogy: every spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal, but not every animal is a dog — explain how this one-directional logic matches squares and rectangles.
Attempt counterexamples: draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle, and try to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle (explaining why the last is impossible).
activities.insight: Class inclusion is one-directional: 'all A are B' does not mean 'all B are A'. The subset asymmetry follows from the extra defining property, not from which shape is more familiar.

activities.title: Shared versus extra properties across the parallelogram family
steps: List the properties that ALL parallelograms share (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect each other).

For each special case, state the extra property that defines it compared with a general parallelogram: a rhombus adds all sides equal, a rectangle adds right angles, and a square adds both (or just one extra property compared with a rhombus or a rectangle).
Fill a property table (rows = shapes, columns = properties) and confirm that each subcategory keeps every shared parallelogram property and adds its extra constraint.
Transfer the reasoning to a new or less familiar shape: given its properties, say where it belongs in the hierarchy and why, and which properties it inherits.
Justify a subset link in words, e.g. 'why is every rectangle a parallelogram?', using shared properties rather than appearance.
activities.insight: Every special parallelogram inherits all the shared parallelogram properties and adds extra defining constraints (one for a rhombus or a rectangle; two for a square, which is one more than a rhombus or a rectangle); this separates necessary/shared properties from the extra property or properties that name each shape.

activities.title: Convince the shape sceptic
steps: Respond to a sceptic who accepts a hierarchy claim only when it is justified from properties: 'Convince me a square belongs inside the rhombus family.'
Answer the follow-up pressure: 'Then is every rhombus a square?' — explaining why the reverse does not hold.
State, for each claim, which properties make it true and which extra property the reverse would require.
Use a counterexample when the sceptic over-generalises (e.g. produce a rhombus that is not a square).
activities.insight: Being made to articulate and defend each subset link, and to expose the reverse as false, consolidates property-based justification over appearance-based classification.

activities.title: Classify and check the hierarchy
steps: Drag or place a set of quadrilaterals into nested regions of a hierarchy, putting the square in the intersection of the rhombus and rectangle sets.
Match each shape (parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square) to its extra defining property.
Answer a true/false question on the asymmetry — 'Which is true: all squares are rectangles, or all rectangles are squares?' — and spot the reversal as a wrong option.
activities.insight: Secure recall and correct placement confirm the hierarchy is stable, including the asymmetry and each shape's extra defining property.

checkQuestion: Tell the child: 'Here are two statements — (1) all squares are rectangles, and (2) all rectangles are squares. One is true and one is false.' Ask: 'Which one is true? And how do you know — what makes it true and the other one false?'
checkAnswer: Statement (1) is true, statement (2) is false. A square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus the extra property that all four sides are equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle. A rectangle only becomes a square when it gains that extra property of equal sides, which most rectangles do not have — so not every rectangle is a square.
